analysis.one_liner: Lets states cap interest rates on loans made by banks and credit unions they charter themselves.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee advanced an amended version of the bill by a 31-18 vote on September 16, 2026; it now waits for a vote by the full House.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law lets a bank charge borrowers anywhere the interest rate allowed in the state where the bank is chartered, even if the borrower's own state caps rates. This bill would let a state opt out of that rule for loans made by banks and credit unions the state itself charters, so those loans would have to follow the state's rate limits. Loans from banks chartered in other states would still be governed by their home state's rules. The bill also repeals a 1980 provision and applies the new rules to any state law or voter-approved provision already adopted under it [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers in states that choose to opt out, especially people taking high-rate loans from banks, credit unions, or online lenders operating through that state's own charters. In an opting-out state, those lenders could no longer charge rates above the state's limits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers in states that opt out

how_it_helps.text: A state could, by adopting a law or by certifying a provision its voters approved, declare that federal rate-exportation preemption no longer applies to loans made by insured banks and credit unions chartered by that state; those loans would then be subject to the state's interest-rate rules.

The opt-out would apply to all loans made by, or committed by, the state's own chartered institutions after the state acts, ending those institutions' ability to export their home state's rates anywhere.

The bill repeals the 1980 provision it amends around and states that the new rules govern the legal effect of any state law or voter certification already adopted under that 1980 provision, so states that acted previously are covered.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit unions chartered in states that opt out, and consumer or online lenders that route loans through those charters, would lose the ability to charge rates above state caps. Some lower-credit-score borrowers could see fewer high-rate loan offers as a result.

drawbacks.text: The opt-out reaches only loans made by the state's own chartered institutions. Banks chartered in other states could keep exporting their home state's rates into an opting-out state, so the largest credit card issuers, which are chartered in states with no rate caps, would be untouched.
Protection would depend on each state acting. In states whose legislature never adopts an opt-out law and whose voters never approve one, nothing changes for borrowers.

Lenders and their trade groups argue that limiting the ability to charge rates above state caps reduces access to credit for higher-risk borrowers; that trade-off would fall mainly on people with low credit scores. Supporters of rate exportation consider this the cost of rate caps generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain for borrowers is real but modest: it only applies in states that affirmatively opt out, and it covers only loans from the state's own chartered institutions. The design leaves the dominant credit card market - issuers chartered in no-cap states - fully outside the reach of state caps, so the biggest channel for high-rate lending to consumers is untouched. A bill focused squarely on borrowers would have let opt-outs reach out-of-state lenders too; this bill trades that away in exchange for letting states control their own charters.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee voted 31-18 on September 16, 2026 to report an amended version to the full House, which has not yet voted on it.

narrative.text: Representative Warren Davidson introduced the bill in the House on March 9, 2026.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
On September 16, 2026, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill to be reported, as amended, by a vote of 31 to 18.
Seven members cosponsored the bill, split between 3 Republicans and 4 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the outcome is open. The bill advanced out of committee with a broad vote, but until it is signed into law, lenders keep their current ability to export rates and the status quo continues unchanged.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders chartered in states with no rate caps
industries.note: The bill leaves out-of-state banks' right to export their home state's rates completely intact, locking in the dominant credit card model even as it lets states rein in their own lenders. Those issuers' profits depend on charging rates above the caps set in borrowers' home states.

industries.industry: State-chartered banks and credit unions in states that opt out
industries.note: In an opting-out state, these lenders would have to follow state rate caps on all loans they make, ending their ability to export rates. Their gain under current law comes from charging more than the borrower's state would allow.

industries.industry: Online and consumer lenders using bank charters (rent-a-bank model)
industries.note: High-rate online lenders commonly route loans through charters of banks in states with few or no rate limits. If a charter state opted out, those loans would become subject to that state's rate caps.

analysis.trajectory: The bill cleared committee with a strong vote, which puts it ahead of most legislation, but it still needs to be scheduled for a vote by the full House and then pass the Senate before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Many committee-approved financial bills never get floor time, so the most likely outcomes are a House floor vote late in the session or the bill quietly expiring at year's end.
